# Apocalypse of Peter — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (attributed to the apostle Peter) |
| **Date** | c. 100–135 CE |
| **Audience** | Greek-speaking Christians, probably in Egypt or Syria |
| **Genre** | Apocalypse / vision narrative / tour of the afterlife |
| **Timeline** | Early second century; one of the earliest extended Christian accounts of heaven and hell |
| **In One Sentence** | A guided tour of heaven and hell, narrated by Peter receiving revelation from the risen Jesus — cataloguing the punishments of the wicked sin by sin, and the glories of the righteous — that nearly entered the New Testament canon and became the literary ancestor of Dante's Divine Comedy. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Apocalypse of Peter exists in two versions: an Ethiopian (Ethiopic) version discovered in 1910 and published as part of a broader apocryphal collection, and a Greek fragment (the Akhmim Fragment) discovered in 1887 in a tomb at Akhmim in Upper Egypt, buried with a monk. The two versions agree substantially on the hellish punishments but differ on the heavenly vision, with the Ethiopic version being longer and fuller. A brief quotation in Clement of Alexandria (c. 200 CE) also confirms the text's early circulation.

The world behind the Apocalypse is one of intense eschatological concern — a community anxious about judgment, about the fate of the dead, and about the basis on which God will sort the righteous from the wicked. The text belongs to the tradition of Jewish apocalyptic tours of the afterlife: 1 Enoch (chapters 17–19, 21–27) describes Enoch's tour of the places where the dead await judgment; the Apocalypse of Zephaniah describes a similar journey. The Apocalypse of Peter is the Christian heir to this tradition, translating it into a revelatory dialogue between Jesus and Peter set on the Mount of Olives (drawing on Matthew 24's apocalyptic discourse).

The text was composed in the aftermath of the Jewish-Roman wars — the reference to "false Christs" and the apocalyptic discourse echo Matthew 24 and may reflect a community processing the trauma of the 70 CE destruction of Jerusalem or the 135 CE Bar Kokhba catastrophe. The concern with specific categories of sinners and their specific punishments suggests a community policing its own boundaries and identity through vivid imaginative eschatology.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Apocalypse of Peter was written to answer the question that keeps every anxious person awake: what will happen to me after I die, and what will happen to those who hurt me or lived unjustly? The genre of the afterlife tour is perfectly designed to answer both questions: here is what the good experience, here is what the wicked experience, and the categories of the wicked are specific enough that readers can locate their oppressors (and themselves) in the catalogue.

The punishments section is the longer and more detailed. The taxonomy of sins and punishments follows a principle of poetic justice (or, in Latin, contrapasso — the same principle Dante will use 1,100 years later). Blasphemers are hung by their tongues over a pit of fire. Women who adorned themselves for adultery are hung by their hair over boiling mud, while their lovers are hung by their feet, their heads submerged in the mud. Those who lent money and charged interest are drowned in filth. Those who persecuted the righteous are eaten by worms in a place of burning. Murderers are in a pit with the beasts they set upon others.

The purpose is simultaneously consolatory and hortatory. Consolatory: for a community experiencing injustice and persecution, the detailed description of its oppressors' ultimate fate offers genuine comfort — God sees, God knows, God will act. Hortatory: for a community that may be tempted toward various sins (adultery, blasphemy, usury, abortion, apostasy under pressure), the vivid specificity of the punishments provides a deterrent. This is eschatology in service of ethics.

The text also serves a significant secondary purpose: it shows what Peter, the chief apostle, was told by the risen Jesus in private. Like the Gospel of Peter (another second-century Petrine pseudepigraph), it builds Petrine authority by creating a tradition of private revelation to Peter that supplements (or supersedes) the public teaching of the canonical Gospels.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Apocalypse of Peter is not long — the Ethiopic version is 17 chapters, the Akhmim Fragment shorter — and it divides cleanly into three movements.

The first movement (chapters 1–6 in the Ethiopic version) is a paraphrase and expansion of the Olivet Discourse of Matthew 24. Jesus and the disciples are on the Mount of Olives; Peter asks about the end times; Jesus responds with a mixture of canonical and new material. A fig tree parable about the last days follows. This section establishes the genre framework: we are reading an expansion of canonical apocalyptic material, presented as authentic Petrine tradition.

The second movement (chapters 7–12) is the vision of heaven. The descriptions are luminous but relatively brief: the righteous are clothed in light, their faces shine like the sun, their hair is white as roses. Two beautiful men appear — identified as Elijah and Enoch, the two who did not die in the Old Testament — as signs of what the resurrected body will be like. The fragrance of the place, the beauty of the light, the peaceful waters — these descriptions are formulaic but genuinely lovely. The heavenly vision lacks the concreteness of the hellish vision; the positive afterlife is harder to describe vividly than the punitive one.

The third movement (chapters 7–12 in the Ethiopic, the bulk of the Akhmim Fragment) is the tour of hell. This is what the text is famous for, and modern readers should approach it with both moral seriousness and historical awareness. The catalogue of punishments includes: those who spoke wickedness against the way of righteousness; unbelievers; women who committed abortion; those who persecuted the righteous; parents who disobeyed their own parents; false witnesses; those who denied righteousness; usurers; sorcerers; adulterers.

Read each punishment description carefully and notice the contrapasso principle: the punishment enacts in the body exactly what the sin enacted — blasphemous tongues are burned, lustful bodies are exposed and tormented in the manner of their lust, cruel people are subjected to the cruelty they inflicted. This is not random sadism — it is a specific theology of divine justice in which punishment is the full revelation of what the sin actually was.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The literary connection to Dante is real but not direct. Dante's Divine Comedy (1308–1320 CE) draws on the broader tradition of Christian afterlife tours, of which the Apocalypse of Peter is the earliest substantial example. The specific chain runs: Apocalypse of Peter → Apocalypse of Paul (a later, more elaborate tour, c. 380–400 CE) → medieval Latin Vision of Paul → Dante's Inferno. The contrapasso principle, the guided tour structure, the movement from hell to paradise — all of these structural features of the Commedia have their ultimate literary ancestor in the Apocalypse of Peter, filtered through centuries of elaboration.

The Jewish ancestor texts are 1 Enoch (chapters 17–27), the Apocalypse of Zephaniah, and 4 Ezra. The Apocalypse of Peter is the first major Christian adaptation of this Jewish genre, translating it into the framework of Petrine revelation and using it to describe specifically Christian categories of sin and reward.

The abortion passage (the description of the punishment of women who "procured abortions" and of the infants themselves, who are given to an angel for safekeeping and eventual resurrection) is the earliest explicit Christian condemnation of abortion in anything approaching a narrative form. It is not a legal ruling or a theological argument — it is a vivid eschatological image. The passage has been cited in modern Christian debates about abortion, which requires careful historical contextualization: the text reflects second-century Roman moral concern (abortion was widely practiced in the Roman world and regarded by many as morally neutral or even commendable), not modern debates.

The canonical Book of Revelation (Apocalypse of John) and the Apocalypse of Peter were the two apocalyptic texts most seriously considered for the New Testament canon in the second and third centuries, and their fates diverged partly due to geography and tradition rather than obvious theological superiority. Reading the two alongside each other illuminates both.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The moral taxonomy of the punishments is a window into second-century Roman Christian ethical priorities and anxieties. The sins that receive the most elaborate punishments — sexual immorality (multiple categories), usury, abortion, religious persecution, apostasy — are not random. They reflect the specific challenges facing a community navigating between Jewish ethical inheritance (sexual purity, financial justice), Roman cultural norms (sexual liberty, financial practice), and the pressure of intermittent persecution. The text is mapping the community's moral world onto the cosmos.

Modern readers will struggle most with the section on abortion and infant punishment, not merely because of contemporary political associations but because the theological problem is real: what happens to infants who were aborted? The Apocalypse's answer — they are given to a caring angel and will eventually be taken up — is an early and serious attempt to address a genuine theodicy question. The text does not consign them to hell; it places them in a kind of limbo of care while their mothers are punished. This is pastorally complex, not simply sadistic.

The usury punishment (moneylenders drowned in a river of filth up to their knees, while the money they hoarded burns before them) reflects a deep ancient ethical consensus, shared by both Greco-Roman philosophy and Jewish Torah (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:36–37, Deuteronomy 23:19–20), that lending at interest to the poor is a form of exploitation. Medieval Christian economic ethics, which banned usury entirely, drew on this tradition. Modern capitalist finance has completely reversed the moral valuation. Reading the Apocalypse's punishment for usury forces a confrontation with how dramatically economic ethics have changed.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Apocalypse of Peter came very close to being canonical. The Muratorian Fragment (possibly late second century) includes it in its list of accepted texts, though with the note that "some of us do not want it read in church." Clement of Alexandria (c. 200 CE) quoted it as scripture. Eusebius listed it among "disputed" books — not rejected, but contested. In the third and fourth centuries it was clearly considered a potential canonical text by significant Christian communities.

What ultimately excluded it was a combination of factors. Its pseudonymous authorship (Peter clearly did not write it) was eventually recognized. The Book of Revelation, despite its own contested status, eventually prevailed as the canonical Christian apocalypse, making the Apocalypse of Peter redundant within an increasingly fixed canon. Athanasius excluded it in 367 CE, and his 27-book list gradually became normative.

In the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, whose canon is the broadest of any major Christian tradition, the Apocalypse of Peter is not included — but the Ethiopic text tradition preserved the most complete version of it. The text survived, as so many near-canonical texts did, in manuscript traditions at the edges of the canonical mainstream.

The Akhmim Fragment's discovery in 1887 (the same year and the same find also contained a fragment of the Gospel of Peter) generated significant scholarly excitement. Together these two Petrine apocrypha illuminated a second-century tradition of Petrine pseudepigraphy — the construction of a Peter who had private revelations and special authority — that had largely been invisible to modern scholarship.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 100–135 CE | Apocalypse of Peter composed (Greek) |
| c. 150–200 CE | Muratorian Fragment lists it with a note of disputed status |
| c. 200 CE | Clement of Alexandria quotes it as scripture |
| c. 313 CE | Eusebius lists it among "disputed" books |
| c. 367 CE | Athanasius excludes it from his canon |
| c. 380–400 CE | Apocalypse of Paul written — more elaborate afterlife tour — supersedes it |
| c. 500–1300 CE | Various Latin vision texts continue the tradition; reach Dante's era |
| 1308–1320 CE | Dante's Divine Comedy — the tradition's greatest literary fruit |
| 1887 CE | Akhmim Fragment discovered in Egyptian tomb with a monk |
| 1910 CE | Ethiopic text discovered and published |
| 1912 CE | M.R. James publishes English translation, bringing text to wide attention |

---
